summary: Specifies Flexible Algorithm, which lets IS-IS and OSPF compute paths using operator-defined metrics and constraints rather than only the default IGP metric. It also describes how Segment Routing prefix segments can be used with these algorithms to steer traffic along the resulting paths.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9350 lets IS-IS and OSPF compute paths using metrics and constraints beyond the ordinary IGP metric. Routers that agree on a Flexible Algorithm can then use Segment Routing identifiers to forward traffic along those paths.

questions: how to do constraint-based routing in ospf or is-is
how does flex-algo choose a winning definition
what is the flex-algorithm number range
subtitle: How IS-IS and OSPF compute paths using configurable metrics and topology constraints.

tldr.problem: The ordinary IGP metric may not express every traffic requirement, such as minimizing delay or avoiding selected links.
tldr.mechanism: A Flexible Algorithm Definition combines a calculation type, metric type, and constraints. IS-IS and OSPF advertise the definition, and participating routers compute paths using the selected rules.
tldr.outcome: IGPs can compute constrained paths and associate them with Segment Routing identifiers. RFC 9350 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 9843 and RFC 9917.

today: RFC 9350 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9843 and RFC 9917. Read the updates alongside this specification.

sections.title: Why Flexible Algorithms Are Needed
sections.content:
IGPs traditionally calculate paths using the metric assigned to each link. That metric may not reflect every traffic requirement. A path preferred for bandwidth, for example, may not be best for traffic sensitive to delay.

Networks have used RSVP-TE or Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE) to compute paths using other metrics or constraints. RFC 9350 extends IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 so the IGPs themselves can advertise and compute constrained paths.

The RFC also describes how SR-MPLS Prefix-SIDs and SRv6 locators can be associated with a Flexible Algorithm, so they identify paths calculated using its rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A network's usual route metric may not match every traffic need. Flexible Algorithms let routers calculate additional paths using a shared metric and set of link constraints.

sections.title: Algorithm Definitions and Identifiers
sections.content:
A Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD) contains a calculation type, a metric type, and a set of constraints. A Flex-Algorithm is a number from 128 to 255 associated with a FAD through configuration.

The operator defines what each number means. Routers in the same advertisement scope must agree on that meaning so their calculations are consistent and forwarding remains loop-free. Possible constraints include using a particular network plane, using an extended metric, or including or avoiding links with selected affinities.

Participation is configured per router. Not every router needs to participate, and only some participants need to advertise the FAD.
sections.plainLanguage: A Flex-Algorithm number identifies a shared routing recipe: how to calculate a path, which metric to use, and which links to include or avoid. Routers using the same number must agree on its definition.

sections.title: Advertising the Flexible Algorithm Definition
sections.content:
IS-IS advertises a FAD in a sub-TLV of its Router Capability TLV. OSPF advertises it as a top-level TLV in a Router Information LSA. Both formats carry the Flex-Algorithm number, metric type, calculation type, priority, and optional constraint sub-TLVs.

Metric type 0 means the IGP metric, type 1 means minimum unidirectional link delay, and type 2 means the traffic-engineering metric. Calculation type 0 is Shortest Path First. Priority values range from 0 to 255; the numerically greatest value is preferred.

Constraints can exclude or include links based on administrative groups and can exclude Shared Risk Link Groups. A flags sub-TLV carries the M-flag, and Flex-Algorithm link attributes use Application-Specific Link Attribute advertisements unless the IS-IS L-flag calls for legacy advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise the algorithm number, metric, calculation method, priority, and optional link rules. This information gives other routers the inputs needed to compute the same kind of path.

sections.title: Selecting the Winning Definition
sections.content:
Different routers may advertise different FADs for one Flex-Algorithm. Each participating router selects the winning definition with two rules: choose the advertisement with the numerically greatest priority, then break a tie using the numerically greatest IS-IS System-ID or OSPF Router ID.

A router that is not configured to participate ignores FAD advertisements for that algorithm, though it may advertise a definition. A configured router that has no valid FAD, or cannot support part of the winning definition, must stop participating and remove its related forwarding state.

A change to a FAD may trigger network-wide recomputation and temporarily disrupt traffic, similar to other routing convergence events.
sections.plainLanguage: Every participating router uses the same tie-breaking rules to select one definition. If it cannot support the winning rules, it stops participating in that algorithm.

sections.title: Calculating Paths and Pruning Links
sections.content:
A router must be configured to participate and must select the winning FAD before calculating a path. The calculation uses the metric and calculation type in that definition. For SR-MPLS and SRv6, nodes that do not advertise participation are removed from the topology used for the calculation.

Links are pruned in order: first, links matching an excluded administrative-group color; second, links in an excluded SRLG; third, links with none of the include-any colors; fourth, links missing any include-all color. If the algorithm uses a non-IGP metric and a link does not advertise that metric, the link is also pruned; the router must not assume a metric value of zero.

Calculations are limited to one area. For inter-area or inter-domain routes, the local router selects an egress ABR or ASBR, which computes the path through the next area or domain. Without the M-flag and the related prefix metrics, such paths are not recommended because traffic can loop or be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The router removes links that violate the algorithm's rules, then calculates a path using the chosen metric. Because each calculation sees only one area, a route into another area depends on the next area's router.

sections.title: Forwarding with Segment Routing
sections.content:
In SR-MPLS, a Prefix-SID advertised for a Flex-Algorithm is associated with paths computed by that algorithm. The router installs the path using the MPLS label for that Prefix-SID. If no path is available for that algorithm, traffic intended for it must be dropped rather than sent on another path.

In SRv6, each node has a locator for each supported topology and algorithm pair. A locator advertised with a Flex-Algorithm value must use paths calculated by that algorithm. A node must not install forwarding entries for a Flex-Algorithm in which it does not participate.

Loop Free Alternate backup paths must use the same constraints and only identifiers advertised for the algorithm. Other data planes must define their own forwarding behavior separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Segment Routing identifiers direct traffic onto paths computed for a particular algorithm. If that path is missing, the router drops the traffic instead of sending it along a different route.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could advertise a FAD with a higher priority than legitimate advertisements and take control of a Flex-Algorithm definition. An attacker could also falsely advertise that a router does or does not support an algorithm.

Existing authentication extensions for IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 can address these attacks. If an authenticated router is compromised, it can still advertise an incorrect FAD and cause traffic to be misrouted or lost. Authentication does not prevent a trusted but compromised router from sending incorrect routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can protect advertisements from an outside attacker. It cannot prevent a compromised trusted router from advertising a false definition.
